title: When Leaders Turn Communities Over to Drug Addicts
author: Renn, Aaron
summary: Aaron Renn uses The Atlantic's investigation of harm-reduction policies in cities like Seattle and Burlington to argue that a generation of civic leadership failure has produced urban environments where ordinary families cannot safely use parks, playgrounds, or public transit. He documents how harm-reduction philosophy has evolved from needle exchanges into effectively sanctioned open-air drug markets in some cities, and traces this dysfunction to a decades-long hollowing out of civic leadership capacity: the disappearance of rooted families, corporate consolidation, managerialism, and the civic culture collapse accelerated by the Covid and BLM years. Renn argues that the dysfunction is not primarily ideological but structural — there is no longer a class of civic leaders with the standing, the incentives, and the social accountability to make decisions that impose short-term costs for long-term community benefit. The article is a case study in how leadership failure at the civic level produces direct harm to vulnerable populations, including both families and drug-addicted people left to deteriorate in public.
points: Under the philosophy known as 'harm reduction,' some cities have effectively done much more than legalise drugs — they have allowed public drug dealing and consumption, and in some cases are actively underwriting it with city resources.
Drug addicts have taken over parks and playgrounds, making them unsafe for families — in some cases public spaces are literally closed and fenced off because of the volume of drug-related activity.
